name: Alsea

sources.title: After More Than 170 Years, Siletz Tribe To Reclaim Ceded Land
sources.annotation: Interviews and a Siletz council statement connect prospective coastal land return with community memory and stewardship. The article still describes transfer as pending. Its compressed historical chronology is not used to date earlier reservation reductions.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the complete substantive article, lines 63–106, including the pending-transaction paragraph. No photographs, precise parcel location, legal title conclusions or invitation-only access arrangements are reproduced.

claimBlocks.text: The Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians includes Alsea among its ancestral peoples while emphasizing that each has a distinct history, culture and legal relationship. The Tribe also explains that many members identify their ancestry through particular villages or bands. Alsea continuity within Siletz therefore need not erase those more specific family connections, nor imply that the many ancestral peoples became culturally interchangeable.

The Tribe’s account of reservation reduction disputes the official claim that coastal land was unoccupied or unwanted. It specifically describes Alsea and Yaquina villages still occupied by their people during the 1860s. Its later article recounts Yachats residents’ resistance to another removal. Read alongside the federal records, this perspective keeps residents’ presence and objections visible when administrative documents describe land being opened to settlers.

claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Whose Lens? Photography and Representation, pages 3–4
claimBlocks.text: Siletz’s photography lesson identifies Thomas C. Jackson as Alsea, with family from near present-day Waldport. It follows his return to Siletz after studying photography and his work making portraits, community scenes and landscapes. The lesson asks readers to consider how Native people represented themselves and their families, rather than treating every historical photograph as an outsider’s record of disappearance. Jackson’s photographs offer a concrete Alsea connection to that history.

claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Restoration lesson pages 1, 3; Termination lesson pages 2–3
claimBlocks.text: The Tribe’s restoration lesson distinguishes the 1954 termination law from its implementation in 1956. Its account describes the loss of services and land alongside Siletz families’ grassroots organizing to regain federal recognition in 1977. This is a confederated political history relevant to Alsea descendants within Siletz. A change in federal recognition should not be read as the disappearance and later recreation of the people themselves.

Addressing the Senate in 1976, Siletz council member Pauline Bell Ricks described rebuilding the council through elections, meetings and community participation. She explained that people who had moved away for work still understood Siletz as home and returned for gatherings and the restoration campaign. Her testimony adds a participant’s account of continued relationships during termination. It speaks to the confederated community; it should not be recast as testimony from a separately identified Alsea government.

claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Article paragraphs on pending transaction and statements by Alfred Lane IV and Angela Sondenaa, web lines 91–104
claimBlocks.text: An October 2026 report records Siletz officials discussing a proposed coastal land return near Yachats. Council member Alfred Lane IV connects the place with memories of people confined at the Alsea Subagency, while natural resources director Angela Sondenaa discusses renewed stewardship and gathering opportunities. The article describes the transfer as still underway, so it supports a dated account of community priorities and expectations, rather than confirmation of completed ownership or a separate Alsea-only landholding.

scopeAndIdentityNotes: The modern Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians is a government encompassing multiple ancestral peoples, including Alsea. No separate current Alsea government, enrollment count or exclusive descendant roster is asserted.

Alsea people, the Alsea language, the town of Alsea and the multi-people Alsea Subagency are different subjects. Amanda DeCuys is identified by the curriculum as Coos; do not call her Alsea because she was confined at the Alsea Subagency.
The Siletz Dee-ni lessons concern Pacific Coast Dene, not Alsea. General Siletz basketry, ceremonial or seasonal lessons do not automatically document Alsea-specific practices.

Jackson provides the clearest specifically Alsea individual connection in this packet. Ricks’s testimony and the 2026 interviews are explicitly confederated perspectives, not evidence assigning each speaker an Alsea ancestry.

correctionsAndCautions: Renew p11-s3 as the inspected history-series collection and p11-s6 as actual selected curriculum content, without retaining duplicate counted cards for their index/subpages.
Use 1954 law / 1956 implementation / 1977 restoration wording rather than implying one simultaneous termination event in 1954.

The October 2026 news headline and some quotations use return language, but its transaction paragraph explicitly says the transfer is still ongoing. Do not convert it into a verified completed conveyance.

The news story’s compressed explanation links a mid-century reduction with the Rogue River treaty/Franklin Pierce; the Tribe’s separate history specifically dates the relevant Yaquina opening to Andrew Johnson’s December 21, 1865 order. Avoid using the news passage for that chronology.
The curriculum’s analysis of Jackson photographs is useful for representation, but the images themselves were not licensed for republication here.
coverageGaps: Additional public Alsea-descendant perspectives and family-specific continuity could strengthen the profile; no claim that these four units represent all descendants.
Current citizenship rules, population, membership ancestry proportions, legal title or completed 2026 transfer were not independently verified.
No restricted cultural narratives, ancestral-remains discussion, site coordinates, archaeological locations or ceremonial instructions are included.
Federal law, older specialist history, placenames and archival-language coverage belong to the parallel reviewers; this packet does not replace their source checks.
